a: a brother of James
t: Jude, brother of James, brother of Jesus
p: Jude is the Hebrew name Judah. His famous brother James makes him a brother of Jesus too.
b: Ioudas is the Hebrew name Judah. English Bibles spell this writer "Jude" to keep him apart from Judas Iscariot. The Gospels list Jesus's brothers as "James, Joseph, Simon and Judas" (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55). The only James who needed no introduction was James of Jerusalem, "the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19), so Jude is most likely Jesus's brother. Clement of Alexandria (Adumbrationes on Jude) remarks that Jude knew his close relation to the Lord yet called himself not his brother but his servant. What "brother" means is debated: younger sons of Mary and Joseph (most Protestants); sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Eastern Orthodox, a view found from the 100s and later championed by Epiphanius); or cousins (Roman Catholic, following Jerome).
r: Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55; Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13; James 1:1; Luke 6:16; 1 Corinthians 9:5

a: loved in God the Father and kept safe for Jesus Christ
t: Loved in God, kept for Jesus: the letter's thread
p: "Kept" opens a chain of "keep" words that runs through the whole letter, to the last verses.
b: "Loved in God the Father" is unusual Greek: the readers are loved and live within God's own life, not only loved by him. "Kept" is a perfect participle ("kept and still kept") with Jesus Christ in the dative: kept for Jesus, guarded until he comes (most likely), or kept by or in him (KJV "preserved in"). The verb tēreō returns again and again. The angels "did not keep" their rank, so God "has kept" them in chains (Jude 6). Darkness "has been kept" for the intruders (Jude 13). The readers must "keep yourselves" (Jude 21), and God "is able to guard you" (Jude 24). The letter is built on this contrast.
orig: ἐν θεῷ πατρὶ ἠγαπημένοις καὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ τετηρημένοις

a: may they be multiplied
p: "May your peace be multiplied" is the greeting of the royal letter in Daniel 4:1.
b: Greek letters began with "greetings" (chairein). Jewish letters wished "peace" (shalom), and "mercy and peace" was a Jewish blessing (Galatians 6:16). "Be multiplied" comes from the royal letter in Daniel 4:1, a phrase that also opens 1 Peter and 2 Peter. Jude makes a set of three, mercy, peace and love, and two of them return near the end: "God's love" and "the mercy of our Lord" (Jude 21), and mercy again in Jude 22–23.
r: Daniel 4:1; Daniel 6:25; 1 Peter 1:2; 2 Peter 1:2; Galatians 6:16; 2 John 3; 1:21; 1:22–23

a: fight hard for the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all
t: Contend for a faith handed down
p: An athlete's verb, and a teacher's verb: strain every muscle for a faith received, not invented.
b: Epagōnizesthai, found only here in the New Testament, is built on agōn, a sports contest (our "agony"): strain hard on behalf of something precious, not pick a quarrel. "The faith" here is the content of what Christians believe (Galatians 1:23). "Handed down" (paradidōmi) is the word for passing on tradition: "Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua" (Mishnah Avot 1:1), and Paul "handed on" the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3). Hapax, "once for all," means a single, final act, against teachers with new revelations (Jude 8). Protestants often read this as support for Scripture alone as the final standard. Catholic and Orthodox readers note the faith was handed down orally too and see it kept in the church's living tradition.
orig: ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τῇ ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει
r: 1 Timothy 6:12; 2 Timothy 4:7; Galatians 1:23; 1 Corinthians 15:3; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 6:20; 1:8

a: slipped in among you without being noticed
p: The verb pictures someone sneaking in by a side door. Wandering teachers were a known danger.
b: Pareisdyō means to slip in sideways, unnoticed. Paul uses a close cousin for "false brothers secretly brought in" (Galatians 2:4), and 2 Peter 2:1 says false teachers will "secretly bring in" destructive teachings. Early churches depended on traveling preachers and prophets, who could be exploited. The Didache, a church manual from about the same period, says a traveling prophet who asks for money or stays more than two days is a false prophet. Jude's intruders seem to be such visitors: they eat at the church's meals (Jude 12), claim visions (Jude 8), and seek profit (Jude 11, 16).
orig: παρεισέδυσαν (pareisedysan)

a: Their judgment was written down long ago
p: The KJV's "ordained" sounds like predestination. The Greek says "written beforehand," most likely in prophecy.
b: Progegrammenoi means "written beforehand," the verb Paul uses for Scripture (Romans 15:4). Three readings: (1) In prophecy: the judgment was foretold in the texts Jude goes on to cite (Israel, angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah, Enoch, the apostles). This is the view of most modern commentators. (2) In heavenly books: Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch speak of heavenly tablets where deeds and fates are recorded. (3) Predestined: the KJV's "ordained to this condemnation" was read this way by Calvin and others. The text says their judgment was foretold, not that they were forced to sin.
orig: οἱ πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι (hoi palai progegrammenoi)

a: turn the grace of our God into shameless self-indulgence
p: Aselgeia is unrestrained living, especially sexual. The intruders made God's forgiveness a reason to sin.
b: Aselgeia, KJV "lasciviousness," means behavior with no brakes: open, shameless indulgence, usually sexual (Romans 13:13; Galatians 5:19; 2 Peter 2:2, 7, 18). "Turn" (metatithēmi) means to change one thing into another, even to desert (Galatians 1:6). The intruders seem to have taught that grace frees believers from moral rules. Paul fought the same idea: "Should we stay in sin so that grace may multiply? By no means!" (Romans 6:1–2). They kept the word "grace" and changed what it meant.
orig: τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριτα μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν

a: Master
p: Despotēs is a slave owner. Used of a divine master it means God; only here and 2 Peter 2:1 is it clearly Jesus.
b: Despotēs (our "despot") is the owner of a slave, and several New Testament uses are about human masters (1 Timothy 6:1–2; Titus 2:9; 1 Peter 2:18). When it names a divine master, it is a title of God (Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24; Revelation 6:10). Only here and in 2 Peter 2:1 is it clearly given to Jesus. It fits Jude's opening: he is the doulos, "slave," of this Master (Jude 1). One Greek article governs both "Master" and "Lord," so both belong to Jesus Christ. "Disown" likely means denying him by how they live (Titus 1:16). Compare 1 Enoch 48:10, on those who "denied the Lord of Spirits and his Anointed."
orig: τὸν μόνον δεσπότην καὶ κύριον ἡμῶν (ton monon despotēn kai kyrion hēmōn)
r: 1 Timothy 6:1–2; Titus 2:9; Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24; Revelation 6:10; 2 Peter 2:1; Titus 1:16; 1:1

a: Jesus
p: If Jude wrote "Jesus," he believed the one who led Israel out of Egypt was the Son before he became human.
b: The main editions now print "Jesus" here (see the manuscript note). How could Jesus save Israel from Egypt? (1) The pre-existent Son. Jude, like Paul, sees Christ at work in Israel's history: "the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4); "we should not test Christ, as some of them did" (1 Corinthians 10:9). Some scholars connect this with "the angel of the LORD" who led Israel (Exodus 23:20–23). (2) Joshua. In Greek, Joshua's name is also Iēsous (Hebrews 4:8), so some ancient readers took it that way, but Joshua did not bring Israel out of Egypt, so few accept this. (3) If the original is "the Lord," it means God, with no puzzle.
r: 1 Corinthians 10:4; 1 Corinthians 10:9; Exodus 23:20–23; John 12:41; Hebrews 4:8; Hebrews 11:26

a: saved a people out of the land of Egypt
p: Like Paul, Jude uses the wilderness generation as a warning to Christians, not as a charge against the Jews.
b: The story is Numbers 14. Israel was rescued from Egypt, but when the spies returned, the people refused to trust God and enter the land. God swore that the adult generation would die in the wilderness while their children entered. Paul (1 Corinthians 10:1–12) and Hebrews (3:7–4:11, quoting Psalm 95) use the story the same way: being rescued once does not make it safe to stop trusting. The warning is aimed at the church, which Jude treats as heir of Israel's story. It is not a claim that Israel as a people was rejected: the next generation entered the land.
r: Numbers 14:20–35; Numbers 26:64–65; Psalms 95:8–11; Psalms 106:24–26; 1 Corinthians 10:1–12; Hebrews 3:16–19

a: deserted the dwelling that was theirs
p: Jude retells Genesis 6:1–4 the way 1 Enoch does: angels left heaven for human women and were bound in darkness.
b: Genesis 6:1–4 says "the sons of God" took human wives. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36, by the 200s BC) expands this: 200 angels came down on Mount Hermon, took wives, fathered giants and taught forbidden arts. God has their leader thrown "into the darkness" (1 Enoch 10:4) and the rest bound "until the day of their judgment" (10:12), and asks, "Why have you left the high, holy heaven?" (15:3). Isaiah 24:21–22 already pictured the host of heaven shut up in a pit and punished "after many days." Jude's "rank" (archē, also "beginning," hence KJV "first estate") is the post God assigned them (Deuteronomy 32:8; Daniel 10:13). They would not keep it, so God keeps them.

a: everlasting chains down in the gloom
p: Genesis 6 angels, or Satan's rebellion before creation? Christians have read Jude 6 both ways.
b: (1) The Watchers of Genesis 6. The standard reading in Judaism before about AD 100 and among early Christian writers such as Justin and Irenaeus. Most scholars agree this is what Jude meant, since his wording matches 1 Enoch and he quotes 1 Enoch in Jude 14. (2) A fall before creation. From the 100s and 200s, and widely by the 400s, many rejected the idea of angels marrying women. Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai said "sons of God" meant nobles (Genesis Rabbah 26:5), Julius Africanus (about 220) proposed the line of Seth, and Augustine agreed (City of God 15.23). Many Christians then read Jude 6 as Satan's original rebellion (Isaiah 14; Revelation 12). Both readings agree on Jude's point: rebels against God's order are held for judgment.

a: down in the gloom
p: Greek myth chained the rebel Titans in gloomy Tartarus. 2 Peter borrows the word. Jude's source is Jewish.
b: Hesiod's Theogony (about 700 BC) tells how Zeus bound the rebel Titans in Tartarus, a place of murky gloom far beneath the earth. The parallel is real: rebel heavenly beings, chains, darkness, a pit below. 2 Peter 2:4, retelling this verse, even uses the verb tartaroō, "throw into Tartarus." But Jude's own wording ("deserted the dwelling," "the great day" of judgment) comes from 1 Enoch, not Greek myth. Verdict: Jewish writers described the fallen angels in language Greek readers would recognize, but the story's roots are Genesis 6 and Jewish tradition, and its end, a final judgment day, has no counterpart in Hesiod.

a: Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them
p: Ancient writers pointed to the barren, smoking land by the Dead Sea as visible proof of the judgment.
b: Genesis 19 tells how fire fell on Sodom and Gomorrah. The "towns around them" include Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23; Hosea 11:8); Zoar was spared. Jude says they "are set out" (present tense) as an example. The salty, sulfurous country near the Dead Sea looked burned, and writers said so: the Wisdom of Solomon speaks of "a continually smoking wasteland" (10:7), and Josephus says traces of fire could still be seen. Archaeologists have proposed sites such as Bab edh-Dhra near the southern Dead Sea and Tall el-Hammam to the north, but no identification has wide agreement.
r: Genesis 19:24–29; Deuteronomy 29:23; Hosea 11:8; Isaiah 1:9; Amos 4:11; Matthew 10:15; Luke 17:29; 2 Peter 2:6

a: like these gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after other flesh
p: "These" are probably the angels. "Other flesh": desire for angels, same-sex acts, or both?
b: "These" (toutois) is masculine, so not the cities (feminine); most take it as the angels of Jude 6. Then Jude pairs two boundary crossings: angels after human women, humans after angels. The Testament of Naphtali (3:4–5) likewise pairs Sodom and the Watchers, who both "changed the order of nature." Heteros means "other, different" (KJV "strange flesh"). Readings: (1) Angels: the men of Sodom demanded Lot's guests, who were angels (Genesis 19:1–11). Many recent commentators (Bauckham, Davids, Green). (2) Same-sex acts: the traditional reading, in Philo and many church fathers, comparing Romans 1:26–27. (3) Both: attempted gang rape of men who were, unknown to them, angels. The Bible also names Sodom's pride and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50).
orig: τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις ... ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας

a: the punishment of eternal fire
p: Sodom's fire went out long ago. Is it "eternal" in its effects, or a picture of a fire that never ends?
b: The Greek can be read "an example of eternal fire" or "undergoing the punishment of eternal fire." Either way, the fire that ended Sodom previews the last judgment (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Traditional view (most churches): final punishment is conscious and unending, and Sodom illustrates it. Conditional immortality (Edward Fudge; John Stott, tentatively): Sodom's fire was "eternal" because its result, total destruction, is permanent, so final punishment may be destruction rather than endless pain. Both sides use this verse, and both take judgment seriously.
r: Matthew 25:41; Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 14:10–11; Revelation 20:10; 2 Peter 2:6

a: dreamers
p: Not daydreamers. In the Greek Old Testament this word is used for false prophets who claim revelations.
b: Enypniazomai means to have dreams or visions. In the Greek Old Testament it describes the prophet or "dreamer of dreams" who leads Israel after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5) and false prophets who say "I had a dream!" (Jeremiah 23:25). The intruders probably claimed visions that authorized their freedom. The KJV's "filthy dreamers" adds a word not in the Greek (printed in italics). Jude may also mean they live in a dream world, but the prophetic background is stronger.
orig: ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι (enypniazomenoi)

a: set aside lordship, and slander the glorious ones
p: "Glorious ones" are angels. "Lordship" may be the Lord's own authority or a rank of angels.
b: Kyriotēs, "lordship," can mean (1) the authority of the Lord Jesus, whom they "disown" (Jude 4), the reading many commentators prefer; or (2) a rank of angels, "dominions" (Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21). Doxai, "glories," are glorious beings, angels, as the next verse shows (also 2 Peter 2:10–11). Why insult angels? One suggestion: Jews believed the Law was given through angels (Galatians 3:19; Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2), so people who thought themselves free of the Law might mock its angelic guardians. The three charges (stain, set aside, slander) answer the three examples of Jude 5–7. The "slander" words (blasphēmeō) then run through Jude 8, 9 and 10.
orig: κυριότητα ἀθετοῦσιν, δόξας βλασφημοῦσιν
r: 1:4; Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21; 2 Peter 2:10–11; Galatians 3:19; Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2

a: Michael the archangel
p: Michael ("Who is like God?") is the angelic prince of Israel in Daniel and the dragon's opponent in Revelation.
b: Mikha'el means "Who is like God?" In Daniel he is "one of the chief princes" and "the great prince who protects your people" (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1). In Revelation 12:7 he leads the war against the dragon. "Archangel" appears only here and in 1 Thessalonians 4:16. Jewish writings list him among four or seven chief angels (1 Enoch 20; 40:9). Jude's point depends on his rank: if even the highest angel would not insult the devil, what are these people doing slandering angels?

a: disputing about the body of Moses
p: This story is not in the Old Testament. Early church writers said Jude took it from the Assumption of Moses.
b: Deuteronomy 34:5–6 says God buried Moses and "No one knows the place of his grave to this day." Origen (On First Principles 3.2.1) and other early writers say Jude's story came from a book called the Assumption (or Ascension) of Moses. A Jewish work on Moses's last words survives in one damaged Latin manuscript in Milan (now usually called the Testament of Moses), but its ending is lost. Later Christian writers preserve pieces of the burial scene: the devil claimed the body, accusing Moses of murder (Exodus 2:12), or claiming all matter as his own. Michael answered only with the words the LORD speaks to Satan in Zechariah 3:2, "The Lord rebuke you." See the note on Jude 23.

a: he did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him
p: Either Michael would not insult the devil, or he would not presume to convict the devil of slander himself.
b: The Greek krisin blasphēmias is literally "a judgment of slander." (1) A slanderous verdict (KJV "railing accusation"): Michael would not use insulting language even against the devil. (2) A verdict for slander: the devil was slandering Moses as a murderer, and Michael did not presume to sentence him for it, because judgment belongs to God (Bauckham). Either way, Michael left judgment to the Lord.
orig: οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας

a: as animals that cannot think do
t: What they know and what they don't
p: A wordplay: they don't "know" spiritual things, but they "grasp" their appetites, like animals, and that ruins them.
b: Jude uses two verbs for knowing. What they do not know (oidasin), the unseen world of angels and God's order, they insult. What they grasp (epistantai) "by nature" (physikōs), like aloga zōa, "animals without reason," they indulge, meaning food and sex. And by those things "they are ruined" (phtheirontai, also "corrupted"). People who claim higher insight live below the human level. 2 Peter 2:12 expands this: "like animals born to be caught and destroyed."
orig: φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα (physikōs hōs ta aloga zōa)

a: the road Cain walked
p: To Jews of Jude's time, Cain was more than a murderer: he was the first to teach that there is no judgment.
b: "Woe" is a prophet's cry of doom (Isaiah 5:8–23; Matthew 23:13–36), and the three past tenses that follow treat the intruders' ruin as already done. Genesis 4 tells of Cain's jealousy and murder of Abel. Jewish interpreters saw more. In the Aramaic Targums (Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan) on Genesis 4:8, Cain says, "There is no judgment, no judge, no world to come." Philo made Cain the picture of the self-lover (That the Worse Attacks the Better 32, 78), and Josephus says he grew greedy and taught others wickedness (Antiquities 1.60–61). In the New Testament, Cain "belonged to the evil one" (1 John 3:12). So "the road Cain walked" fits teachers who deny judgment and lead others into sin.

a: Balaam's error
p: Balaam took money to curse Israel and then, says Numbers 31:16, taught Moab how to lead Israel into sin.
b: Balaam was hired by King Balak of Moab to curse Israel (Numbers 22–24). God turned his curses into blessings, but Numbers 31:16 says Balaam's advice led Israel into the sexual sin and idol feasts at Peor (Numbers 25). Later writers remember his greed (Deuteronomy 23:4; Nehemiah 13:2; 2 Peter 2:15–16) and his teaching (Revelation 2:14). The Mishnah contrasts the disciples of Abraham with those of Balaam, who have "an evil eye, a haughty spirit, and a broad soul," that is, a greedy one (Avot 5:19; 5:22 in some editions). "Thrown themselves" is literally "poured themselves out": they gave themselves over to it, for pay.
orig: τῇ πλάνῃ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ μισθοῦ ἐξεχύθησαν
r: Numbers 22:1–24:25; Numbers 25:1–3; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 23:4; Nehemiah 13:2; 2 Peter 2:15–16; Revelation 2:14

a: Korah's revolt
t: Korah: talking back to God's servant
p: Korah challenged Moses and Aaron, and the ground swallowed his followers. Jude's word means "talking back."
b: In Numbers 16, Korah, with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders, challenged Moses and Aaron: "All the congregation is holy!" The ground swallowed the rebels, and fire consumed the 250. Jude's word antilogia means "speaking against." The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel's quarrel at Meribah, "the water of contradiction" (Numbers 20:13, Septuagint). The Mishnah calls Korah's band the classic "dispute not for the sake of heaven" (Avot 5:17; 5:20 in some editions). Korah's sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), and eleven psalms carry their name (Psalms 42, 44–49, 84–85, 87–88).
orig: τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κόρε (tē antilogia tou Kore)

a: sunken rocks
p: Spilades are rocks just under the water that wreck ships. The KJV's "spots" comes from a similar word.
b: In Greek writers, spilas is a rock or reef hidden below the surface, dangerous because it cannot be seen. That fits people who "slipped in among you without being noticed" (Jude 4) and can wreck the church's fellowship. The KJV's "spots" follows a later meaning and the similar word spiloi, "stains," which 2 Peter 2:13 uses in its parallel. Jude may intend the echo: in Jude 23 he uses the verb "soiled" (spiloō). Most modern translations prefer the rock image.
orig: σπιλάδες (spilades)

a: love feasts
t: The love feast, and bad shepherds
p: Early churches shared a real meal, the agapē, with the Lord's Supper. The intruders "shepherd themselves" there.
b: The plural agapai, "loves," is the earliest use of the word for the church's fellowship meal. Christians met in homes and ate together, rich and poor at one table, and the Lord's Supper was part of the meal (1 Corinthians 11:17–34). Ignatius (about AD 110) uses agapē for it, and Tertullian (about 197) explains that it is named for love and feeds the poor. The intruders feast "without fear," without reverence (1 Corinthians 11:27–30), and "shepherd themselves," the charge Ezekiel 34:2 brings against Israel's leaders: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been shepherding themselves!" They seem to have acted as teachers.
r: 1 Corinthians 11:17–34; Acts 2:42–46; 2 Peter 2:13; Ezekiel 34:2–10; John 10:11–13; 1 Peter 5:2–3

a: waterless clouds
p: Clouds, trees, waves, stars: sky, land, sea and heavens. 1 Enoch also contrasts obedient nature with sinners.
b: "Clouds and wind, and yet no rain: / that is someone who boasts of a gift that is a lie" (Proverbs 25:14). These teachers promise refreshment and deliver nothing. Jude adds three more pictures, one from each part of the world: clouds in the air, trees on land, waves of the sea, stars in the sky. The waves recall Isaiah 57:20: "the wicked are like the churning sea... its waters churn up mud and slime," the scum a storm leaves on a beach. The opening of 1 Enoch (chapters 2–5) tells readers to look at sky, earth and sea, which keep God's order, while sinners do not, and 1 Enoch 80 adds that in sinners' days rain will fail and stars will stray.

a: late-autumn trees with no fruit, dead twice over, torn up by the roots
p: Trees bare at harvest time, then uprooted: fruitless and finished. It may also hint at the second death.
b: Phthinopōrinos means "late autumn," the end of harvest, when trees ought to have fruit. The KJV's "whose fruit withereth" guesses from a related verb meaning "waste away." "Dead twice" may mean (1) dead both ways, fruitless and rootless; (2) people who came alive from sin, then died again; or (3) facing the "second death" (Revelation 2:11; 20:14). Jesus used the same pictures: a good tree bears good fruit (Matthew 7:17–19), and "Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted" (Matthew 15:13).
r: Matthew 7:17–19; Matthew 15:13; Luke 13:6–9; John 15:6; Revelation 2:11; Revelation 20:14

a: wandering stars
p: "Planet" comes from this Greek word. In 1 Enoch, stars that left their courses are punished angels.
b: Asteres planētai, "wandering stars," gives us "planet." Ancient sky-watchers saw that a few lights did not move with the fixed stars. In 1 Enoch, stars that "did not come out at their proper times" are bound in a dark, empty place (1 Enoch 18:13–16; 21:1–6), and in Enoch's animal vision the fallen Watchers appear as falling stars (86:1–3). The Bible too links stars and angels (Job 38:7; Isaiah 14:12; Revelation 1:20; 9:1). So the intruders, like the angels of Jude 6, have left their course, and "the gloom" kept for those angels is kept for them too.
orig: ἀστέρες πλανῆται (asteres planētai)

a: also prophesied about these people
p: Jude 14–15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9, a book not in most Bibles, introduced by its own title, "the seventh from Adam."
b: Enoch is seventh in Genesis 5 counting Adam; he "walked with God... for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). "The seventh from Adam" is 1 Enoch's own label (60:8). Jude then quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a passage also preserved in Aramaic among the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q204, 4QEnoch-c). Views: (1) Genuine prophecy. Jude, like many Jews then, accepted it as Enoch's. Tertullian defended 1 Enoch partly because Jude quoted it, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church still has it in its Bible. (2) A true word in a non-biblical book, as Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). The most common Protestant and Catholic view. (3) His readers' book: Jude quoted what they respected. Jerome says some rejected Jude because of this quotation.

a: The Lord has come with his holy ones by the tens of thousands
p: A prophetic past tense; "the Lord" added by Jude, probably meaning Jesus; and "holy ones" are angels, not "saints."
b: Ēlthen is a past tense, "came": Hebrew prophets often tell a sure future event as already done (KJV "cometh"). The surviving Greek and Ethiopian texts of 1 Enoch 1:9 say "he comes," meaning God; Jude has "the Lord," which in Jude usually means Jesus (Jude 4, 17, 21), so Enoch's coming of God becomes the coming of Jesus (1 Thessalonians 3:13; Matthew 25:31). The "holy myriads" (a myriad is 10,000) are angels, as in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Zechariah 14:5, which 1 Enoch echoes. The KJV's "ten thousands of his saints" is not wrong, since "saint" means "holy one," but modern readers hear "Christians."
orig: ἰδοὺ ἦλθεν κύριος ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ
r: Deuteronomy 33:2; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 7:10; 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 2 Thessalonians 1:7; Matthew 25:31; 1:4; 1:17; 1:21

a: all their ungodly deeds that they did in their ungodliness
p: Four "ungodly" words in one sentence (three in NA28). It is Jude's key word, and why he chose this quotation.
b: The asebēs word family ("ungodly, irreverent") appears four times in this verse in the SBLGNT (three in NA28; see the manuscript note): "the ungodly... ungodly deeds... in their ungodliness... ungodly sinners." Jude called the intruders "ungodly" in Jude 4 and will again in Jude 18. Jewish teachers often linked passages by a shared key word, a method later called gezerah shavah. Jude's word ties his picture of the intruders to Enoch's prophecy: the same people, the same verdict. The "harsh words" spoken "against him" lead straight into Jude 16.
orig: ἀσεβεῖς, ἀσεβείας, ἠσέβησαν, ἀσεβεῖς

a: grumblers who complain about their lot in life
p: The Greek word for grumbling is the word for Israel's complaining in the wilderness, the generation of Jude 5.
b: Gongystai, "grumblers," echoes the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel's complaining in the desert (Exodus 16:7–12; Numbers 14:27–29), the generation that died in the wilderness (Jude 5). Paul makes the same link: "do not grumble, as some of them did, and were destroyed" (1 Corinthians 10:10). Mempsimoiroi means "blaming one's fate," always discontented with one's share. Greek moralists knew the type; Theophrastus sketched the chronic complainer as a character.
orig: γογγυσταί, μεμψίμοιροι (gongystai, mempsimoiroi)

a: Their mouths speak puffed-up words, and they flatter people to get what they want
p: Big talk like Daniel's arrogant king, and favoritism toward people who can pay them back.
b: Hyperonka means swollen, inflated. Theodotion's Greek version of Daniel uses it for the king who "will speak monstrous things against the God of gods" (Daniel 11:36; compare Daniel 7:8). "Flatter" is literally "admiring faces for the sake of advantage," a Greek form of the Hebrew idiom nasa panim, "lift the face," to show favoritism (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17; a related idiom in Deuteronomy 1:17; James 2:1–9). Bauckham notes close parallels in the Testament of Moses, which Jude knew (Jude 9): "their mouth will speak great things" (7:9) and "admiring persons" (5:5).
orig: λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα, θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα ὠφελείας χάριν
r: Daniel 7:8; Daniel 11:36; Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 1:17; James 2:1–9; 2 Peter 2:18

a: the words spoken beforehand by the apostles
p: Jude does not count himself an apostle. He quotes what the apostles "kept telling" his readers.
b: Jude speaks of the apostles as a group apart from himself, which counts against the old Western identification of him with the apostle "Judas of James" (Luke 6:16), Jude Thaddeus. "They kept telling you" (Jude 18, an ongoing past tense) suggests the readers had heard apostles in person. The saying itself matches no written text exactly but sums up apostolic warnings (Acts 20:29–30; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5), and 2 Peter 3:3 repeats it, adding what the mockers say: "Where is the promise of his coming?" Traditional view: the apostles were recently active, so the letter is early. Many critical scholars: it looks back on a finished apostolic age, near AD 100.
r: Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13; 2 Peter 3:2–4; Acts 20:29–31; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5; 1:18

a: In the last time
p: The New Testament writers believed the "last time" had already begun with Jesus.
b: "In the last days" was a prophets' phrase for the time God would act decisively (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). The apostles said those days had begun: Peter applies Joel's "last days" to Pentecost (Acts 2:17), Hebrews 1:2 says God has spoken "in these last days" by his Son, and 1 John 2:18 calls it "the last hour." That is why Jude can say of the mockers, "These people" (Jude 19): the prophecy is being fulfilled now.
r: Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18; 2 Peter 3:3; 1:19

a: They are merely natural and lack the Spirit
p: They sort people into classes and claim to be spiritual. Jude says they are "soul-ish" and have no Spirit.
b: Apodiorizontes, "those who mark off," is rare: they split the church, or rank people, treating themselves as the spiritual elite. The KJV's "separate themselves" may follow late copies that add "themselves," or simply read the verb that way. Psychikos, from psychē ("soul, life"), is Paul's word for the person who "does not accept the things of the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 2:14). The KJV's "sensual" meant "governed by the senses" in 1611 but suggests sex today. Jude turns the tables: those who claimed superior insight "lack the Spirit." In the 100s, Gnostic teachers divided humanity into "spiritual" and "soul-ish" classes; Jude may face an early form of that idea, or a pride like Corinth's.
orig: οἱ ἀποδιορίζοντες, ψυχικοί, πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες

a: Pray in the Holy Spirit
p: Pentecostal readers often see praying in tongues here. Others read prayer led and empowered by the Spirit.
b: The intruders "lack the Spirit" (Jude 19); the readers pray "in the Holy Spirit." Pentecostal and charismatic readers often connect this with praying in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:14–15: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with my mind also"). Most other interpreters read it broadly: prayer prompted and empowered by the Spirit, who "helps us in our weakness" (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18). The Greek does not settle the question.

a: Keep yourselves in God's love
p: Building, praying and waiting describe how; the only command in Jude 20–21 is "keep yourselves."
b: In Greek, "build" and "pray" (Jude 20) and "look forward" are participles; tērēsate, "keep," is the only command. The church builds on its faith like a building on a foundation (1 Corinthians 3:9–17; Ephesians 2:20–22), and does it together ("yourselves" is plural). God's love here is most likely his love for them, the place they stay in, as in "remain in my love" (John 15:9–10). Notice the shape of Jude 20–21: the Holy Spirit, the love of God, the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ, an early naming of Father, Son and Spirit together (compare 2 Corinthians 13:14).
orig: ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ τηρήσατε

a: look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ
p: The mercy they wait for is what Jesus will show when he returns to judge.
b: "Look forward to" (prosdechomai) is the word for people waiting for God's kingdom (Luke 2:25, 38; 23:51) and for Christ's appearing (Titus 2:13). Paul prays that Onesiphorus "may find mercy from the Lord on that day" (2 Timothy 1:18). The scene is the coming Enoch described (Jude 14–15): judgment for the ungodly, mercy for those who keep themselves. Mercy runs through the letter: wished (Jude 2), awaited (Jude 21), and passed on to others (Jude 22–23).

a: those who waver
p: Diakrinomai can mean "doubt" or "dispute." Jude used the same verb for Michael's "arguing" in Jude 9.
b: Diakrinomenous usually means "wavering, doubting" in the New Testament (Matthew 21:21; Romans 4:20; James 1:6). But the same verb means "dispute" in Jude 9, where Michael was "arguing" with the devil. So Jude may mean (1) have mercy on those who waver, unsettled by the intruders (most translations); or (2) on those who dispute with you, possibly the intruders themselves, the reading of Richard Bauckham and Jerome Neyrey. The KJV's "making a difference" follows a different Greek text (see the manuscript note).
orig: διακρινομένους (diakrinomenous)

a: and hate even the tunic the flesh has soiled
t: Snatched from the fire, stripped of filthy clothes
p: Back to Zechariah 3: the high priest is "a stick snatched from the fire," and his filthy clothes are removed.
b: In Zechariah 3:1–5 the high priest Joshua stands in filthy clothes, accused by Satan. The LORD says, "The LORD rebuke you, Satan!" (Zechariah 3:2), words Michael uses in Jude 9, and "Is not this man a burning stick snatched from the fire?" (compare Amos 4:11). Then the filthy clothes are taken off. Jude uses both pictures. The chitōn was the tunic worn next to the skin, and Zechariah's Hebrew word for "filthy" is related to the word for excrement. Jude's point: rescue people urgently and show mercy, but carefully, because sin is contagious. Compare Revelation 3:4, "a few names in Sardis who have not dirtied their clothes."

a: the tunic the flesh has soiled
p: My reading: Jude frames his letter with Zechariah 3, whose accused high priest is named Iēsous in Greek.
b: This is my theory, one idea in two parts. First, Jude places the two halves of Zechariah 3 at the two ends of his argument: Michael will not accuse but leaves judgment to the Lord (Jude 9), and believers rescue from the fire and strip the soiled clothing (Jude 23). The readers are to be rescuers, not accusers. Second, in the Greek Old Testament the high priest of that scene is named Iēsous, the same name as Jesus. Greek-speaking readers who heard "Jesus saved a people" (Jude 5, if original) might connect the two. Commentators such as Bauckham note both Zechariah echoes; reading them as a deliberate frame, and the link to the name, are my own suggestions.

a: guard you from tripping
t: Kept on your feet, presented without a flaw
p: God can keep his people from falling, and present them like a perfect offering.
b: Aptaistous means "not tripping," like a sure-footed animal on rough ground: "He will not let your foot slip" (Psalm 121:3; compare Psalm 56:13). After a letter full of people who fell (Israel, angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah), Jude ends with the God who keeps his people standing. "Without a flaw" (amōmos) is the word for a sacrificial animal with no defect (Exodus 29:1; Leviticus 1:3), used of Christ (1 Peter 1:19) and of the church he presents (Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22). It answers the intruders, who are rocks or "spots" (Jude 12) with soiled clothing (Jude 23). "Shouting for joy" (agalliasis) is exultant, celebrating joy.
orig: φυλάξαι ὑμᾶς ἀπταίστους ... ἀμώμους ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει
r: Psalms 121:3–8; Psalms 56:13; Exodus 29:1; 1 Peter 1:19; Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22; 1:12; 1:23

a: the only God, our Savior
p: "God our Savior" is an Old Testament title. Jude calls God "only," as he called Jesus "only Master" in Jude 4.
b: "Savior" is a title of God throughout the Old Testament: "a God who is righteous and saves; / there is none except me" (Isaiah 45:21). Mary sings of "God my Savior" (Luke 1:47), and the letters to Timothy and Titus use the phrase often. Jude's "only" is pointed: there is one God, and in Jude 4 Jesus is the "only Master." Glory goes to the only God "through Jesus Christ our Lord": early Christians worshiped the one God of Israel through Jesus. A doxology (from doxa, "glory") like this closes many letters (Romans 16:25–27; 1 Timothy 1:17), and Jude's is one of the best known, often spoken as a blessing at the end of services.
orig: μόνῳ θεῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν (monō theō sōtēri hēmōn)
r: Isaiah 45:21; Luke 1:47; 1 Timothy 1:1; 1 Timothy 1:17; Titus 1:3; Romans 16:25–27; 1:4
